flawed_step: The key exchange step fails: you cannot justify that some optimal schedule contains the shortest interval. Swapping the shortest interval into an optimal schedule can mean removing two optimal intervals, because a short interval can overlap the end of one interval and the start of the next.
counterexample: Take the intervals A=[0,10), B=[9,12) and C=[11,20), with lengths 10, 3 and 9, all different. Greedy first picks B, the shortest. B overlaps A (they share [9,10)) and overlaps C (they share [11,12)), so both are thrown out and greedy ends with 1 interval. A and C do not overlap, so {A,C} is a valid schedule of size 2. Since all lengths differ, ties never come up, and greedy gets fewer intervals than the best schedule.
assessment_summary: To prove the claim, I tried the usual exchange argument: show that some optimal schedule contains the shortest interval I, then repeat on what is left. That step cannot be justified. I can overlap two intervals of an optimal schedule that do not overlap each other, so swapping I in can lose one interval. The three intervals [0,10), [9,12), [11,20) show this: greedy gets 1, the best schedule has 2, and ties play no part because all lengths differ. The statement is false.
